stories.title: Somali piracy surges as the impact of the US-Iran war ripples outwards
stories.summary: Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, Pirates manage to board ships operating a long way from the coast and then guide them closer to the shore By Barbara Plett Usher Africa correspondent Published 29 August 2026, 02:14 BST A surge in piracy near Somalia has increased threats to shipping already under pressure from maritime blockades and conflict due to the US war with Iran. Two cargo vessels were seized in the Gulf of Aden within four days last week, rising to at least 13 the number of ships attacked since the start of the year and triggering unprecedented drone strikes against the pirates. It is the biggest escalation in hijackings in more than a decade, renewing concern about security in this region vital to international trade. "Piracy is always a crime of opportunity," says Omar Mahmood, a senior Somalia analyst for the International Crisis Group (ICG), "and right now the pirates see an opportunity." That opportunity comes from the impact of the war on regional waterways further north. Iran and the US continue to battle over control of the strategic Strait of Hormuz. And Tehran's Houthi allies in Yemen have imposed a targeted blockade in the Bab al-Mandab Strait, which controls access to the Red Sea.

Publié le : 29/08/2026 - 00:01 2 min Temps de lecture Le marché de Geidam, ville du nord du Nigeria, le 22 juillet 2023. © Wikimedia Commons CC BY-SA 4.0 AuntyAfrah Par : RFI avec AFP Publicité Lire la suite Des jihadistes de la Province de l'État islamique en Afrique de l'Ouest (ISWAP) ont attaqué dans la nuit de mardi à mercredi une base militaire à Geidam, une ville d'environ 89 000 habitants, provoquant une fusillade qui a duré jusqu'à l'aube, selon des habitants. L'État de Yobe, tout comme l'État de Borno voisin, a été l'un des plus durement touchés par le conflit jihadiste qui dure depuis 17 ans au Nigeria. « Nous sommes contraints de rester chez nous depuis mercredi par les soldats, qui ont averti tout le monde de ne pas mettre le nez dehors », a déclaré à l'AFP par téléphone Abubakar Musa, un habitant de Geidam. Deux officiers militaires ont expliqué que le couvre-feu était nécessaire, car les jihadistes ont assiégé la ville et pourraient lancer de nouvelles attaques. « Les terroristes ont été repoussés, mais ils sont revenus et encerclent la ville de Geidam depuis mercredi : impossible d'y entrer ou d'en sortir », a affirmé un militaire. « Les terroristes sont cachés à l'extérieur de la ville et les soldats ne peuvent patrouiller qu'à l'intérieur de la ville. La situation est donc vraiment critique », a ajouté un autre officier.

In a seven-page press release on Thursday night, 27 August 2026, Eskom conceded it had made R3-billion in irregular payments to its diesel suppliers. It stopped short of calling these prepayments - as amaBhungane's investigation has alleged - instead referring to "advanced payments" and "payments outside of contractual terms". The flurry of payments was made to three suppliers between January and April 2025, when Eskom was faced with a return of load shedding. "The period between January and March 2025 placed significant demands on the power system and required rapid operational responses and difficult decisions by employees and executives to maintain security of supply and protect grid stability," Eskom CEO Dan Marokane said in the statement. "However, operational pressures do not diminish our obligation to comply fully with internal controls and governance requirements." Eskom said that it had occasionally made prepayments to diesel suppliers in the past to stave off load shedding, adding: "This may have contributed to advance payment being viewed as an available operational mechanism. stories.summary: https://p.dw.com/p/5JZrB Over 800,00 people are estimated to have been murdered in the 1994 Rwandan genocide Image: DW Advertisement A Rwandan-born Dutch national was on Friday sentenced to life imprisonment by a court in the Netherlands for his role in the 1994 Rwandan genocide . The Hague District Court found that the 66-year-old man, identified only as Eugene N., had taken part in attacks on homes in Tutsi communities and thrown a grenade into a crowd of Tutsis sheltering in a football stadium, and convicted him of war crimes and genocide. "The conduct of the defendant establishes a significant lack of respect for human dignity and for human life," read a statement from the court issued after the conviction. "Only a lifelong prison sentence does justice to the immense suffering that has been inflicted on the victims and the bereaved families." Handing down the verdict, the presiding judge said N.'s actions were committed with "genocidal intent." Rwandan genocide: How many people died? During the 1994 genocide in Rwanda , more than 800,000 Tutsis and moderate Hutus were killed in a campaign of mass murder orchestrated by Hutu extremists. Many leaders of the slaughter were tried and convicted by a United Nations war crimes tribunal that has now closed down. N. was sentenced for his role in the massacre of around 3,000 Tutsis in Mbazi in southern Rwanda in April 1994, in which prosecutors said he was "personally involved." "If the horrific crimes of the suspect, in which not one but an estimated 3,000 innocent people were literally slaughtered, in which the suspect personally threw a grenade into a stadium, do not deserve a life sentence, then what does?" one prosecutor asked the court.

"If you came out and started running, they shot you." The gunmen, who struck at 02:00, split into groups to surround residents: one at the village entrance, one in the centre and one at the back. "They opened fire without a care in the world, shooting indiscriminately," the 55-year-old quietly tells the BBC World Service. It was one of many attacks that have caused havoc in the mainly Muslim community where residents live in fear of being kidnapped for ransom. Fatima explains how the raids unfold: "You could have 100 motorcycles, and each one could be carrying three people." About 70 people, including children, were killed from the village of Bia Buki in June, according to Fatima. She describes how the attackers also targeted villagers as they fled and children were injured falling into ditches. Among the dead were her husband and six of his seven siblings.

stories.title: Four arrested over boxing champion's murder in South Africa
stories.summary: Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Zolani Tete was in training for a comeback fight when he was killed By Khanyisile Ngcobo ,Â Reporting from Johannesburg Â and Â Jude Winter ,Â BBC Sport Published 24 August 2026 Four people have been arrested in South Africa in connection with the murder of boxing champion Zolani Tete, who was shot dead outside his home on Friday. Tete, 38, was gunned down in what has been described as an ambush in Mdantsane, Eastern Cape. A young woman who was with him was also shot and is in hospital. One of the men being held, a 22-year-old who was arrested on Saturday, will make an initial appearance in court on Monday, and faces murder and attempted murder charges. Tete held the WBO bantamweight title from 2017 to 2019, as well as the IBF super-flyweight title in 2014.

Photograph: EvritFilms Review On Different Grounds review – Cupid’s-conspiracy romcom brings Nollywood and Bollywood together Mildred Okwo’s earnest film about the conflicting romantic wishes in a Nigerian family struggles to connect with its promising premise I t’s a stretch for this Nigerian romcom to bill itself “the first Nollywood-Bollywood collaboration” based on the fact that it features, in Nimesh Diliprai Desai and Vineet Raina, two fringe Indian players on a sprawling wedding-invite list. But the two industries do indeed have much common ground, such as big-hearted family values and a penchant for grand gestural emotions that, in the case of Mildred Okwo’s somewhat heavy-footed film, trample on some promising concepts and narrative plausibility. Silk-tressed bachelorette Aurora (Abena Akuaba) is being browbeaten by her businessman dad Eyimofe (Bob-Manuel Udokwu) to marry snoozefest suitor Tobore (Ifeanyi Kalu).

The incident occurred less than a week after the government announced plans to close the ⁠site and relocate the waste because of the threat it posed, especially during the rainy season, which causes landslides and fatal flash ⁠floods each year in crowded, underdeveloped cities across parts of West Africa . The landslide took ​place at about 2am (3am UK time) ‌in the Gbessia commune ‌of Conakry, according to a government statement.

stories.title: Did a goat herder's lucky $200 nugget spark a gold rush in western Kenya?
stories.summary: Image caption, Manasse Lomachar would like the discovery of gold to improve life in his village By Akisa Wandera Published 23 August 2026 A goat herder from a remote area of western Kenya has told the BBC his discovery of a golden nugget has sparked a gold rush, overwhelming his small village over the last few weeks. When people found out that 33-year-old Manasse Lomachar had sold his three grams of gold for 36,000 Kenyan shillings ($280; Â£205) several weeks ago, he believes this led to the arrival of thousands of prospectors in Cheporor. And it is true that what last month was just bushland and rough grazing ground near the village is now scarred by pits, mounds of earth and makeshift mining camps. It is not clear if was Lomachar's lucky find or other recent discoveries that sparked the excitement. But local authorities estimate that about 10,000 people arrived at the height of the rush.
